turns.speaker: A
turns.text: People often say German watches and Swiss watches have a different character. Can you describe the difference?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: I'll try. Watches from Saxony, especially from Glashütte, usually feel calm and serious. You see large plates, like the three-quarter plate, untreated German silver and gold chatons with blue screws.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: It is. Some people call it austere beauty. Austere means plain and strict, without unnecessary decoration. The beauty comes from proportion, quality and careful finishing.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Classic Swiss movements often use many separate bridges with elegant curves. You'll see Geneva stripes, polished bevels and a more open, flowing layout. It feels a bit more like jewelry.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Neither, really. It's a question of taste. Some collectors love the strong, solid feeling of Saxon design. Others prefer the lightness and grace of Swiss work.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: All the time. Many modern makers borrow ideas from both traditions. But when you turn over a watch and see that wide, golden plate, you still know immediately that you're looking at a German way of thinking.
